article_text:
Cannes 2026 is nearing its close, but the Film Comment crew has not slowed down one bit as we continue to cut through the noise with dispatches, interviews, Podcasts, a special Cannes Critics’ Grid, and much more. This year’s edition has been packed with highly anticipated premieres from Ryûsuke Hamaguchi, Valeska Grisebach, James Gray, Paweł Pawlikowski, and many more acclaimed filmmakers.

For our seventh Podcast from the Croisette, FC Editor Devika Girish invited Sight and Sound ’s Thomas Flew and scholar Neta Alexander to discuss a trio of late-festival Competition premieres: Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Palme d’Or–contender Minotaur (3:50); Ira Sachs’s 1980s period drama The Man I Love (18:16); and Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo’s The Black Ball ( La Bola Negra ) (32:48), which received a rousing 20-minute ovation from the Cannes audience.

Next, the group shout out highlights from other sections of the festival: Tom Fontenille’s documentary A Secret Heart (41:52), which premiered in the ACID sidebar; Clio Barnard’s youth-in-England fiction feature I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning (45:20), in the Directors’ Fortnight program; and John Abraham’s newly restored Report to Mother (1986) (47:35), from the Cannes Classics section.

Subscribe today to Film Comment to stay up-to-date with all of our Cannes 2026 coverage.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE : Hollywood vet and Italian native Gianni Nunnari , producer on movies including the 300 franchise , Immortals , and From Dusk Til Dawn , is bringing Brian Selznick ’s ( The Invention of Hugo Cabret ) young adult novel Run Away With Me to the screen, with Selznick adapting his own novel.

Rome-born Nunnari, an exec producer on The Departed and Se7en , will produce through his Hollywood Gang Productions banner, with executive producer set as Deborah Belford de Furia.

Published by Scholastic in 2025, Run Away With Me marked Selznick’s first novel written specifically for a young adult audience. Set in Rome in the 1980s, the queer coming-of-age romance follows Danny, a 16-year-old American spending the summer in Italy, whose life is transformed when he meets Angelo, a mysterious Italian boy. The novel blends more than 100 pages of Selznick’s signature illustrations with prose.

Watch on Deadline

Related Stories

Hollywood Vet Gianni Nunnari & 'Magazine Dreams' Producer Simon Horsman Launch Film & TV Label Euro Gang With Footprints In London, Rome, Madrid & LA; Company Inks Deal With Warner Music Group For Scripted Slate

International Insider: Votes Cast In Israel & Brazil; Tokyo Drift; Domingo Corral Interview

Selznick is the Caldecott Medal-winning author and illustrator of The Invention of Hugo Cabret , which was adapted by Martin Scorsese into the five-time Academy Award-winning film Hugo . His novel Wonderstruck was adapted into the Todd Haynes-directed feature starring Julianne Moore, with Selznick writing the screenplay. His other works include The Marvels , Kaleidoscope and Big Tree , the latter originating from an idea developed with Steven Spielberg.

Nunnari is expected to draw on his longstanding relationships in Hollywood and the European production community to mount the film on location in Rome. He most recently exec-produced Roland Emmerich’s swords and sandals epic Those About To Die in the city. James Canellos and Michael Ritter will also executive produce.

The synopsis continues: “What begins as a chance encounter develops into an intense first love as Danny and Angelo explore the Eternal City together, uncovering stories hidden within its streets, monuments and ruins. Their romance is echoed by other love stories spanning the 17th century, 19th century and 1940s, revealing a history of queer love that has endured even when those relationships were forced into secrecy or erased from the historical record. As the boys grow closer, Angelo’s own secrets begin to emerge, forcing Danny to confront the possibility that their relationship, and the seemingly timeless Roman summer surrounding them, cannot last forever.”

“ Run Away With Me is a universal story of love in the Eternal City, set in the 1980s, when I was falling in love with love and with Rome itself,” said Nunnari. “For me, bringing Brian’s story to the screen feels very personal.”

Selznick added: “I’m thrilled my book is being brought to life by such an extraordinary team. We’re all eager to tell a story that affirms the importance of love, a message that feels more urgent now than ever.”

Executive producer de Furia commented: “ Run Away With Me and Hollywood Gang may seem like an unlikely pairing, but they are a perfect combination. I’ve worked with Gianni for years and have seen firsthand his passion for storytelling, history, love, and Rome, while Brian is one of the most extraordinary creative minds working today and someone I’ve been lucky to know for decades. Run Away With Me pulses with the electricity of first love and the discovery that our own love stories belong to a history much larger than ourselves. And, of course, the Eternal City plays a starring role. Don’t we all want to fall in love in Rome?”

Selznick is represented by CAA.

Tokyo Drift; Domingo Corral Interview", "url": "https://deadline.com/2026/10/israel-brazil-election-international-insider-1237207048/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "塞尔兹尼克是卡尔德科特奖得主的作家和画家《古戈·卡布雷特的发明》 ,由马丁·斯科塞斯(Martin Scorsese)改为五次获得学术奖的电影《古戈》(Hugo) ,他的小说《奇迹》(Wonderstruck)被改为由托德·海恩斯(Todd Haynes)导演的角色扮演朱利安·穆尔(Julianne Moore) ,塞尔兹尼克写了剧本,他的其他作品包括《奇迹》(The Marvels),《卡莱多斯科普》(Kaleidoscope)和《大树》(Big Tree),后者是由史蒂文·斯皮尔伯格(Steven Spielberg)开发的想法产生的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Nunnari 预计将在好莱坞和欧洲生产社区建立长期的关系,以便在罗马拍摄这部电影,他最近制作了Roland Emmerich的剑和三明治,并在城市中制作了《关于死亡的故事》。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“什么开始作为一个机会的约会发展到一个强烈的第一爱,当丹尼和安吉洛一起探索永恒城市,发现隐藏在它的街道,纪念碑和废墟中的故事。 17 世紀, 19 十世纪和 1940 s,揭示了爱情的历史,即使这些关系被强迫秘密或从历史记录中删除,也持续了。安吉洛的秘密开始出现,迫使丹尼面对他们的关系,以及周围的似乎无时的罗马夏天,无法永远持续的可能性。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“与我一起跑步是一部普遍的爱情故事,在1980年代,当我爱上了爱情和罗马本身时,在永恒城里,这对我来说,把布莱恩的故事带到屏幕上,感觉非常个性化。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "塞尔兹尼克补充说:“我很高兴我的书是由这样一个非凡的团队引入生命,我们都渴望讲述一个故事,确认爱情的重要性,一个消息,现在感觉比以往任何时候都更紧迫。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "首席制片人De Furia评论:“与我走路和好莱坞乐队可能看起来不太可能,但它们是完美的组合,我与吉安尼一起工作了好几年,并且首先看到他对故事、历史、爱情和罗马的热情,而布莱恩是今天工作的最非凡的创意思想之一,我已经幸运地认识了几十年的某人。当然,永恒之城扮演着重要角色,难道不是我们所有人都想爱上罗马吗?”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Selznick 由 CAA 代表。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
V iewed from afar, the silver-hued Hami Pterosaur Museum almost looks like a space base on Mars. Viewed from above, it resembles a collection of dinosaur eggs in the sand. Nestled in the Gobi desert, in north-west China , the new tourist attraction showcases hundreds of impressive fossils of pterosaurs, ancient flying reptiles related to dinosaurs. But far from reflecting its prehistoric exhibits, the building itself is a modern-day architectural specimen.

Designed with underground exhibition halls, giant light funnels and sprawling solar farms, the museum is able to operate sustainably while withstanding an extremely harsh environment.

The Hami region is notorious for its scorching summers. Air temperatures can exceed 55C (131F), while the surface ground temperature can reach 80C, says Wang Xiaolin, the director of the museum and a palaeontologist at the Chinese Academy of Sciences. Violent winds and sandstorms terrorise the area frequently, according to Xiaolin, who has carried out excavation work in Hami for 20 years.

Despite the intimidating conditions, building the museum in the area is important from a scientific perspective because this is where the fossils were buried and found, Xiaolin says. Keeping the fossils local protects the fragile relics and lets visitors see them in their geological context, he adds.

Visitors to the five exhibition halls can expect to see precious fossils discovered by Xiaolin’s team, including one that has preserved the upper and lower jaws, as well as the soft-tissue structures of the head crest of a pterosaur that roamed the area roughly 130m years ago.

Most of the 8,000-sq metre museum is built 8 metres into the ground where temperatures are much lower, which helps it stay cool in summer, says Huai Kaifeng, an architect at Beijing-based Turenscape, which designed the project. In winter, when temperatures can drop below -20C, the design also helps the museum stay warm.

Being largely underground, with seven above-ground entrances, allows the museum to use its energy as efficiently as possible, says Wang Yujia, a landscape architect and associate professor at the University of Nebraska–Lincoln in the US, who is not involved in the project. Most of it is able to avoid direct exposure to wind, sand and solar heat and the large temperature swings between day and night in the desert. “This all means that you need much, much less air-conditioning,” Yujia says.

Although air-conditioners have been installed to provide backup, the museum has natural ventilation shafts that allow cool air to sink and hot air to rise and escape. The museum can cut its electricity usage on air conditioning by 94% compared with an above-ground counterpart, according to estimates by Turenscape. This equates to a saving of 223,421kWh of electricity annually – enough to power an average UK home for 89 years.

But the underground space in the desert presented another challenge for the architects: lighting. The team used giant, translucent, ceiling-to-floor funnels to let in as much natural light as possible. These structures slash the museum’s need for artificial lighting by nearly 50%, saving 84,672kWh of electricity a year, according to Turenscape.

The museum was one of the last designs completed by the late Chinese landscape architect Kongjian Yu , the founder of Turenscape. Yu was the brain behind China’s “ sponge cities ”, a concept that uses nature to prevent flooding in urban areas.

after newsletter promotion

The museum has its own micro power grid, featuring a solar farm and batteries to store energy. The solar farm is about 1km from the museum, with an outline resembling that of a pterosaur when viewed from above. It is expected to generate more than 22.4GWh of electricity a year, enough to meet the museum’s own demand, Huai says. The museum is still connected to the power grid of the nearby city of Hami to ensure its energy security, he notes.

The museum is also connected to Hami’s water-supplying network, but it has a recycling system on site to collect, process and reuse its grey water.

“Water is precious out here in the Gobi,” Xiaolin says.

For Yujia, the museum is a good example of how a building can be designed to adapt to its natural environment rather than fight against it.

Although technology enables people to build luxury resorts in a desert and keep them cool, such projects require huge amounts of energy and resources, he says.

“It makes sense to work as much as possible with the environmental conditions that are already there, instead of relying entirely on technology to isolate the building from them.”

Examples include a floating exhibition pavilion built in Rotterdam to address rising sea levels, and a giant park with a tilted ground in Bangkok that aims to prevent urban flooding, and a home shaped like a snail’s shell in Iran to help its inhabitants stay cool.

The concept is important for arid areas. “These places are not cities, you don’t necessarily have the basic infrastructure or the resources you desire even if you pay, because money is not magic,” Yujia adds.

Designing buildings and parks to combat natural disasters was a lasting theme throughout Yu’s career, and for Jiinyi Hwang, the chief architect at Turenscape, the museum is no exception.

“Our world is drying. Deserts and arid zones are expanding. Cities are warming. More and more of the built environment is being pushed into climates that were once considered unbuildable,” Hwang says. “If we keep designing with the same assumptions – sealed boxes, glass facades and mechanical climate control – we will consume the very resources these landscapes cannot spare.”

article_text:
Alex Gibney goes into four hours of detail in his documentary Musk . Over the end credits, songwriter Daniel Pemberton and singer David Byrne summarize Elon Musk in one song, “Let Me Sell You a Dream.”

In a virtual Q&A at Deadline’s Sound & Screen Film event, they shared how the song’s title and chorus encapsulate the mogul.

Related Stories

‘Musk’ Review: World’s Richest Man, And His Digital Avatar, Thrashed In Damning Alex Gibney Doc – Venice Film Festival

‘Project Hail Mary’ Composer Daniel Pemberton Built “A Language From The Ground Up” Using New Instruments – Sound & Screen Film

“We had this one idea of let me sell you a dream, which was the way in,” Pemberton said. “How do you encapsulate who Musk is? At the end of the day I think he’s an amazing salesperson who sells these dreams that are maybe not really reality.”

Byrne remembers recognizing the line during their brainstorming session. The two musicians met outside a London coffee shop.

“Somewhere in our conversation there, that phrase came up, let me sell you a dream,” Byrne said. “And I thought, ‘There’s our chorus. That’s our chorus line right there.’”

Pemberton also composes the score for the entire film. He needed a song to bring the energy back up at the end.

“There was a Flaming Lips song,” Byrne said. “It was very dreamy. Daniel said to me, ‘I think we need something really upbeat and hard-hitting after that. We don’t want to end on this floating dreamy note. We want to just then hit with something hard, grab your attention and bring the energy at the end.’”

Gibney suggested Byrne, Pemberton remembered. Given Byrne’s career with the band Talking Heads, as a solo artist and filmmaker, Pemberton agreed.

“I think David is a generational commentator and observer,” Pemberton said. “We sat outside the coffee shop and I literally played this early idea in my head off my phone to him, and that got us talking. We went back to my studio. We looked at a few things but then we worked very remotely and we talked about the idea for the song. Then David just ran with it.”

Byrne was previously Oscar nominated for his song “This Is a Life” with Ryan Lott and Mitski for the Best Picture Oscar winner Everything Everywhere All at Once . After Musk . He is open to more film work.

“My phone’s right there,” Byrne said. “If I get the calls then who knows what can happen? A lot of those were the same kind of thing. Somebody calls up and goes hey, do you think you can do this?”

article_text:
Born in Paris in 1953, Sophie Calle has spent nearly half a century turning her own life, and the lives of strangers, into material for art. Back in Paris in the late 1970s after years of travel, she began following people in the street, then invited strangers to sleep in her bed for “Les Dormeurs” (1979) and trailed a man all the way to Venice for “Suite vénitienne” (1980). In 1981, she took a job as a chambermaid in a Venetian hotel to photograph the belongings of its guests for “L’Hôtel.” Combining photographs and texts, her projects explore surveillance, intimacy, absence and loss, from “Les Aveugles” (1986), in which people born blind described their image of beauty, to “Prenez soin de vous,” shown in the French Pavilion at the 2007 Venice Biennale. She received the Hasselblad Award in 2010.

This segment comes from “Between Worlds,” an episode of the twelfth season of Art21’s documentary series “Art in the Twenty-First Century,” which premiered on PBS in October 2025. It follows Calle from the Musée Picasso in Paris, where she staged “À toi de faire, ma mignonne” in 2023, to the cryptoporticus of Arles, the ancient Roman galleries beneath the town hall where, for the 2024 Rencontres d’Arles, she left photographs from “Les Aveugles,” already damaged by humidity, to finish decaying.

14 minutes, in English.

article_text:
「 Fly to the Moon: 月をめぐる５つの物語」が 2027 年 1 月 11 日まで、群馬県渋川市の「原美術館 ARC」 で開かれています。

同館は上毛三山のひとつ、榛名山の山麓に位置することから、秋の観光シーズンには、美術とともに自然も楽しみに来たり、伊香保や軽井沢などへ向かう途中に立ち寄る人が多く、担当の山川恵里菜学芸員は「旅」をテーマにした展覧会を思いついたそうです。旅について思いを巡らすうちに、膨らんだ想像力は地球を飛び出し、月見の季節ということもあって、「月世界旅行」にまで広がりました。同館の収蔵品から月にまつわる５つの作品を選んでメインに据え、その作家が活動した時代の社会情勢や、ライバルたちがどのような表現を追究していたのかなど、その作品の周辺を回っていくっていうようなイメージで構成されています。

それでは、ひとつずつ物語を巡って行きましょう。

Episode 1 ロバート・ラウシェンバーグ《ブースター》（1967年）とポップアート

最初の作品はロバート・ラウシェンバーグ《ブースター》（1967年）です。ラウシェンバーグは、第二次世界大戦後に発達したロケットや飛行機など 、スピードのある移動手段と、自分の身近にあるものを組み合わせることで、今の自分やアメリカの一番リアルな部分を表現しようと試みた作家です。 当時は米ソ冷戦時代で、両国は宇宙開発で競い合っていました。それまで 月や宇宙は手が届かない存在でしたが、急に身近になり、自分の生活の一部になり始めていたという背景があります。

この作品は新しい「肖像画」を目指したもので、伝統的な肖像画が 「外面を飾る」のに対し、レントゲンで「内面」を晒しながらも、 ここにはラウシェンバーグの気持ちや表現したいことは何も入っておらず、作家の内面や表現したいものもよく分かりません。大量生産・大量消費が加速し、作っては捨てる時代に、訴求性よりも淡々と自己を表現示する姿勢が見えるクールな作品です。

この作品の周りには、大量生産・大量消費の時代の象徴である自動車を描いたピーター・スタンフリの作品や、ウレタン製の柔らかいネジなど価値観を揺さぶるようなクレス・オルデンバーグの立体作品のほか、ロイ・リキテンシュタインやアンディ・ウォーホルらによる米国のポップアートも紹介されています。

Episode 2 野口里佳《潜る人》（1995年）と日常に潜む光の痕跡

野口里佳《潜る人》は、日常生活の中で酸素ボンベを背負った人と遭遇した奇妙な体験から着想を得た作品です。日常から、異世界や宇宙へ向かう人物を追うような視点で撮影され、日常に潜む非日常感や光の反射、不思議な光景が巨大な画面で表現されています。《潜る人》シリーズは、本来全9点の写真で構成される作品ですが、今回は作家 本人と相談を重ね、 7点を選んで展示しています。

ほかに再開発により変わりゆく東京の下町の風景を撮影した荒木経惟《「アラーキーレトログラフス」展より（冬へ）》を展示しています。

Episode 3 菅井汲《月》（1957年）と日本のアンフォルメル

1960年代、米国ではポップアートが、欧州（特にフランス）ではアンフォルメルが生まれていました。フランスに留学した菅井は、その影響を受けつつも、日本の古代を意識した東洋的な主題をプリミティヴな抽象で表現した《月》などで、パリの画壇に強いインパクトを与えました。

アンフォルメルは、勢いや形 にならない自分の感情を乗せていくようなアート思考です。 白髪一雄は、天井からロープでぶら下がって裸足で描く「フット・ペインティング」で知られ、自身の行為を絵画として定着させることを重視しました。

Episode 4 倉俣史朗《How High the Moon》（1986年）と浮遊する家具

《How High the Moon》は、インテリアデザイナー・ 倉俣史朗のデザインを代表する椅子です。 素材には、建築現場の足場や溝の蓋などに使われる工業素材であるエキスパンドメタル（金属の網）を使用しています。 大量生産される重厚な素材をあえて使い、曲線で構成することで、重力を感じさせない軽やかな印象を生み出しています。

ここでは同館所蔵の倉俣史朗の家具や、親交のあった磯崎新や宮脇愛子の作品、太陽の動きを写真で捉えた野村仁の写真作品が取り合わされます。

Episode 5 《武蔵野図屏風》（江戸時代）と古今の月の表現

特別展示室 觀海庵では、「万葉集」や「続古今和歌集」などで月の名所として繰り返し詠われてきた武蔵野を描いた《武蔵野図屏風》（江戸時代）のほか、工芸品に意匠として組み込まれた月の表現を現代美術作品と交えて紹介しています。

Epilogue 三島喜美代《Newspaper-84-E》（1984年）

三島喜美代は、 新聞や空き缶など身近な大量生産・消費物を、硬質な陶器で大きく再構成し、消費への意識を促す作品を制作しました。回廊エリアにある 《Newspaper-84-E》は、1 984年のニューヨーク・タイムズ紙に掲載されたスペースシャトル「ディスカバリー号」打ち上げニュースを掲載した新聞を題材にしています。 作品は大判の陶板にシルクスクリーンでプリントし、意図的に、くしゃっとさせてから焼成しています。

東京から美術館までは、およそ150kmの距離。秋が深まるなか、小旅行の行き先のひとつにアートを加えてみてはいかがでしょう。（美術展ナビ編集班・若水浩）

article_text:
Ella Fleck at Ehrlich Steinberg

The raised platform in the middle of British artist Ella Fleck’s installation vibrates under your feet to the sound of a male voice. He’s whispering sweet nothings, intoning sexual fantasies. It’s all based on third-party agencies that manage OnlyFans accounts, interacting with users, creating fictional relationships that horny guys spend thousands on. It’s a greasy, gross, uncomfortable exploration of sex work on an industrial scale.

Yuli Serfaty at Xxijra Hii

Yuli Serfaty’s headless metallic dog sculptures guard this booth, their claws sharp, their heavy teats dragging on the floor. It’s a surreal symbol of femininity pushed to an extreme, a body devalued and exploited. A video shows the creature trying to escape the booth, and succeeding. The whole installation looks like HR Giger meets Wolfenstein 3D, but with a nasty, satirical edge.

Rirkrit Tiravanija at David Zwirner

Finally, something to help you get through Frieze. Thai artist Rirkrit Tiravanija’s sculpture here is a robotic arm that carefully hands visitors a little red-and-white ibuprofen pill. If you don’t reach out, it just drops it on the floor. The robot does its job, over and over, regardless of if you’re there to receive it. It feels futile, obscene, repetitive, meaningless. Quite the comment on modern life.

Carolyn Lazard at Trautwein Herleth

It might look like a display of pens, and that’s because it is. But each one is a promotional item from a pharmaceutical company, given out as gifts to American medical professionals. Lazard bought them in estate sales from real doctors. They become a portrait of selling out, of how healthcare in the US can be bought by corporations. There are pens with branding for antidepressants, ADHD meds, Viagra: corporations are keeping you going, keeping you productive. When it clicks, it’s an incredibly grim conceptual vision of how our bodies are treated as commodities.

Gray Wielebinski in the toilets

The urinal cakes in the Frieze bogs this year aren’t just there to keep whiffs at bay – they’re art. This is urinal cake as sculptural intervention, thanks to artist Gray Wielebinski, who has designed each one with a custom scent and encased them in metal cages. They sort of look like little chastity devices, glistening lumps of odorous chemicals for you to wee on. They’re weird, almost erotic sculptures. You can hear the anguished cry of thousands of artists wishing they’d thought of it first.

Miriam Cahn at Galerie Jocelyn Wolff

There is such an overwhelming amount of (usually very bland) painting at Frieze that it really takes a special painter to stand out. But Swiss artist Miriam Cahn’s installation is a proper diamond among the swill. It’s a whole booth filled with 26 years’ worth of self-portraiture. Each one plumbs new depths of anxious, monstrous introspection. She grins and screams, stands and falls, all in blurred, messy washes of colour. Psychologically intense, overwrought, emotional stuff.

William-Adolphe Bouguereau at Stair Sainty

My love for 19th-century French academic painter William-Adolphe Bouguereau verges on a sickness. I mean, I have a Bouguereau tattoo. So finding this little gem among the Dutch flower paintings and Egyptian busts of Frieze Masters was a genuine thrill. It’s a weird, yellowed little thing – based on a Tintoretto – of a man lying prostrate on the ground. The ropes that bind him have been snapped, wood is splintered. Here is the aftermath of violence, the shocking silence after a traumatic event. This is one of the great things about Masters: getting to spot art historical gold hidden away on the back wall of some booth. This gallery also had a gorgeous James Tissot portrait. It’s 19th-century art nerd heaven.

after newsletter promotion

Luce Turnier at Harlesden High Street

There are some amazing narratives to discover in the Frieze Masters spotlight section, especially the work of Haitian modernist Luce Turnier, who lived between Paris and Haiti but has largely been forgotten by art history. This small display of stark portraits – like a more sombre Alice Neel – and vitrines is a little glimpse into a lost period of international modernism from an artist who feels ripe for a museum show.

Camarasaurus supremus skull at David Aaron

You eventually go antiquities and Flemish art blind walking around Frieze Masters, so finding the fossilised dino skulls that David Aaron Gallery has lugged to the tent is always a bit of Jurassic relief. This year they’ve brought an enormous triceratops skull and an awesome camarasaurus supremus with the tooth of an allosaurus embedded in it. Absolutely brutal, and possibly the only thing my four-year-old would like in either fair.

Sohrab Hura at Experimenter

There’s death and fear written into all of Sohrab Hura’s paintings here. They’re grotesque expressionist scenes of everyday violence: a man kicked to the ground, a crow pecking at a bleeding carcass above a figure staring aghast at a newspaper. It’s like Edvard Munch but with way more blood and guts. The painting of the woman in the dust storm isn’t good, but the rest are great, angry things.

article_text:
The Sharjah Intl. Film Festival for Children and Youth will bring films from Thailand, Brazil, India, Italy and across the Arab world to the UAE for its 13th edition, with a lineup featuring international festival titles, emerging filmmakers and Emirati talent.

Running Oct. 26-Oct. 31, SIFF’s Green Carpet program includes Chayanop Bunprakob, Baz Poonpiriya and Atta Hemwadee’s Thai drama “ Gohan ,” Fabrizio Cattani’s Italian feature “Forever With You” and Verena Fels’ Austrian-German animated film “ Monster Mia ,” all receiving their Middle East premieres.

Related Stories

New York's AMC Kips Bay Theater Closes on Jan. 3; CEO Says 'AMC Wants to Stay' but NYU Langone 'Wants Us Gone'

“Gohan” follows a stray dog as he passes through the lives of three owners over more than a decade, while “Forever With You” follows two friends whose search for a missing dog leads them deep into the woods and into unexpected danger. “Monster Mia” follows a 12-year-old girl who finds herself at a school full of monsters. Poonpiriya previously directed Thai box-office hit “Bad Genius” and Sundance prize winner “One for the Road.”

Elsewhere in the lineup, Juan Cabral’s Argentine feature “Risa and the Wind Phone” receives its Gulf premiere. Cabral’s previous feature, “ Two/One ,” premiered at Tribeca and was released by Mubi across select international territories.

Indian filmmaker Ravi Nimbalkar’s “87 Rupees Ink Pen” also receives its Middle East premiere, while Brazilian director Celia Catunda’s animated feature “My Grandfather Is a Nihonjin” arrives in Sharjah after premiering at Annecy in 2025.

The animation selection extends to David Súkup, Patrik Pašš, Leon Vidmar and Jean-Claude Rozec’s Czech-French-Slovak-Slovenian stop-motion feature “ Tales From the Magic Garden ,” another 2025 Annecy selection.

Local talent features in the shorts program. Abdulrahman Al Madani’s “Oug,” part of the Arabic short-film competition, follows an Emirati couple facing family and social pressure to have children. The film received the Gulf Capital-ADMAF Visual Arts Award in 2025 and has since screened at Denmark’s Odense Intl. Film Festival.

Young filmmakers also get their own space through SIFF’s Child & Youth Made Films and student competitions, with selections spanning live-action and animation.

The wider festival program counts 71 films from 38 countries selected from a pool of 1,802 submissions representing 72 countries, with a further eight films screening out of competition. Morning screenings at VOX Cinemas City Centre Al Zahia are reserved for school-aged and university students, while evening screenings are open to the public.

Workshops introduce young participants to stop-motion and flipbook animation, alongside workshops on cinematography, production management and content creation.

Italy, this year’s country of honor, is represented in the workshop program with “The Italian Eye – Photography Through Light, Color & Composition” and “Tell a Story in Five Shots – Inspired by Italian Cinema.”

The festival’s panel lineup turns to what happens once filmmakers have industry-ready work. “Film Festivals Decoded: What Happens After You Press Submit?” brings together festival programmers and directors to discuss the selection process, submissions and how festivals build their programs. Moderated by Saudi Cinema Assn. CEO Hani Al Mulla, the panel features Rotterdam Arab Film Festival artistic director Rosh Abdelfattah, American Intl. University Kuwait executive director of alumni affairs and strategic events Alia Al Azzeh, and Alexandria Short Film Festival head Mohamed Mahmoud.

Another panel, “How Do I Get My Next Film Made? From Idea to Financing,” will focus on pitching materials, development labs, producers, financing and co-production opportunities. The festival’s Industry Hub and pitching sessions will run alongside the public program, giving emerging filmmakers opportunities to present projects and connect with industry professionals.

SIFF opens Oct. 25, with screenings beginning Oct. 26 and continuing through Oct. 31, ahead of the closing ceremony on Nov. 1.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Oscar nominee Amanda Seyfried is set to star opposite Ramy Youssef and Sharon Stone in Martha & Muhammad , the new A24 comedy marking Youssef’s feature directorial debut.

Plot and character details are being kept under wraps. Youssef is directing from his own script, with his Cairo Cowboy producing alongside Eli Bush, Ronald Bronstein and Josh Safdie for Central; Christopher Storer and Tyson Bidner for American Light & Fixture; and A24, which is financing the project.

Seyfried was recently seen starring opposite Sydney Sweeney in Lionsgate’s hit thriller The Housemaid , based on the New York Times bestseller by Freida McFadden. Last year, she also played the title role in Searchlight’s Shaker Movement musical The Testament of Ann Lee .

Seyfried most recently wrapped production on the musical feature Octet from Hamilton ‘s Lin-Manuel Miranda. She will next be seen opposite Scoot McNairy in The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd , directed by Tim Blake Nelson.

Watch on Deadline

She is repped by Innovative Artists and Frankfurt Kurnit Klein & Selz.

article_text:
New York Newsletter

Live From the Lavender Lake

Dispatches from open studios events across town and the Tompkins Square Dog Halloween Parade.

I generally spend a decent amount of time in Gowanus, but weaving through the neighborhood’s streets and buildings for Open Studios on Saturday really demonstrated how the stretch of water has shed its sardonic designation of “ Lavender Lake ” and turned into a bizarro landscape of glimmering apartment buildings. The canalside Whole Foods is one thing, but the “luxury” high-rises boasting an “iconic” view of the waterfront in its funky fluorescence are still a head-scratcher for me.

Now, I’m neither a chemist, an architect, nor a physician, but I’m willing to bet that everyone probably would have benefitted from waiting for water remediation and sewage overflow prevention efforts to be completed instead of developers speedrunning the area’s sublimation from a Superfund site with a petering industrial profile to a bunch of towers offering studio apartments starting at $3,200/month.

Unless there’s a large band of civilians seeking front-row seats to Gowanus’s next poonami … Because they’re literally installing permanent picnic tables and reclining deck chairs along the banks of the canal.

At landscape painter Elizabeth O’Reilly’s studio on Union Street, I commented that she and a few other artists I’d dropped in on were kind for drawing inspiration from the neighborhood as it is. I find it endearing that they’re able to extrapolate beauty at both ends of the spectrum of devastating human impact — from a life-threateningly toxic pollution hub to a shiny new playground for gentrification to mall-ify eventually — and help others appreciate the importance of archiving it.

Keeping things coastal, contributor Aaron Short dropped in on the open studios programming in Red Hook and Sunset Park respectively. Short reports that Red Hook’s creative community barrels forward unabated 13 months after a five-alarm fire tore through a historic warehouse filled with converted artist studios, and that spaces in Sunset Park are somehow still affordable. On the other end of the borough, local artist Jazmine Hayes details the historical, spiritual, and environmental symbolism throughout her Percent for Art commission at the new Brownsville Multi-Service Center.

Since we’re talking about the environment, let’s add some animals to the mix, too. Those who foolishly missed the annual Tompkins Square Dog Halloween Parade can peruse some highlights courtesy of staff writer Anna Lee, who dropped to ankle level for Pup Leo and Santa Paws, among other costumed canines. There are also only a few days left to catch Cannupa Hanska Luger’s American Traditional, which is closing on the 24th at Garth Greenan Gallery’s new location on Greene Street. The show was highlighted in our round-up of New York exhibitions embodying Indigenous survivance, and Editor-at-Large and Co-Founder Hrag Vartanian attests that it’s Luger’s “strongest work yet.”

Lastly, take a glance at our “What Else is Happening?” section — I’ve got some neat stuff lined up for you.

While I can't promise it'll hold a candle to the Dog Parade, Hyperallergic 's own Halloween Party next Wednesday is just the place for your niche, art-world costume to shine during an open bar. Calling all Kusama pumpkins and Magritte apple-faced individuals to the fore! (Discounted tickets available for members. RSVP here !)

13 Art Films to See at DOC NYC

I’ve never put much thought into how I want to be portrayed after I die. Perhaps I’d opt to be plastered on Etsy mugs, tea sets, and journal covers, à la Frida Kahlo (though I doubt I’d have many buyers, or that Kahlo would’ve enjoyed how her self-image is often nowadays detached from the politics and life behind it), or I would begin things early by enlisting an artist to paint their best guess at my posthumous body. Maybe I’d like to be dipped in ink and stamped onto rice paper, as Molly Tenzer does with the roadkill she finds on New York City streets.

The lineup at this year’s DOC NYC, which returns to venues throughout the city from November 11 through November 29, offers many reflections on this question. | Anna Lee

From Our Critics

Hrag Vartanian

Cannupa Hanska Luger: American Traditional at Garth Greenan Gallery

"The artist sets aside the participatory, ceramics-heavy projects he’s best known for and arrives at something more declarative — a synthesis of wood, ink, and archive that is his strongest work yet."

Channelle Chevelle Russell

Deana Lawson: Edge Control at Gagosian

"Lawson’s newest series provokes a fraught ethical question: Who truly has the power to authorize or deny access?"

Gregory Volk

Tanya Merrill: Land animal, house animal at 303 Gallery

"Merrill decisively challenges a pervasive anthropocentric worldview that deems humans superior and animals lesser. She foregrounds local animals as sentient beings with their own motivations and desires."

John Yau

David Reed: Terrible Idea at Rodder

"For more than five decades, he has continued to explore the brushstroke in all its possibilities … In these explorations, one can track his pursuit of color interactions as well as his dialogues with other artists from different epochs."

News

The Metropolitan Museum of Art in Manhattan and the Musée du Louvre in Paris are joining forces to co-organize a major exhibition exploring Greco-Roman and biblical influences throughout Rembrandt’s practice.

NYC Health + Hospitals’ Arts in Medicine department wraps up conservation work on three New Deal-era murals and a John Rhoden sculpture held at its Harlem hospital.

Three New York City agencies unveil a new $128 million multi-service center in Brooklyn’s Brownsville neighborhood, featuring an extensive public art commission by local artist and community educator Jazmine Hayes.

What Else is Happening?

Pablo Helguera needs your help in building Fonoteca, a new public vinyl library for Latinx music! This Wednesday at CUE Art, Helguera is trading limited-edition works and original drawings for donated or loaned vinyls across salsa, bolero, cumbia, merengue, tango, Latin jazz, and more. (Wed Oct 21) [ cueartfoundation.org ]

This Thursday at Smack Mellon, performance artist Asia Stewart becomes a table in “any experience with men and alcohol,” an experiential endurance work dissecting service and power through audience participation. (Thu Oct 22) [ smackmellon.org ]

Of Life, Liberty, and a Pursuit of Happiness is a one-day symposium at Brooklyn Museum, in which participants including Sky Hopinka, Viva Ruiz, Qween Jean, Dean Majd, Yomaira Figueroa-Vásquez, Mariame Kaba, and Chelsea Manning reckon with the most urgent issues in our sociopolitical landscape. (Fri Oct 23) [ creativetime.org ]

The Center for Art, Research, and Alliances is hosting a launch party for the Robert Blackburn Printmaking Workshop's inaugural publication, Common Ground , celebrating master printer Mohammad Omer Khalil's earlier namesake exhibition. (Sun Oct 25) [ rbpmw-efanyc.org ]

At the Brooklyn Academy of Music, queer theorist Jack Halberstram, who authored Anarchitecture After Everything (2026), and Avgi Saketopoulou will discuss the radical reenvisioning of the body and the structures and systems it operates in through the lens of transness. (Tue Oct 27) [ bam.org ]

It's still early days for On Self-Respect , a group exhibition at Land to Sea cafe showcasing a variety of work on identity, self-perception, and memory, rooted in the namesake 1961 essay by Joan Didion. On view through December 18! [ instagram.com ]

article_text:
The weekend feels awards-y with John Turturro tugging the heartstrings in The Only Living Pickpocket in New York , Olivia Colman ( Wicker ) and Helen Mirren ( A Talent For Murder ) in the house, and Hans Zischler and Sandra Hüller playing Thomas Mann and his daughter on a road trip ( Fatherland ). The A24 You Can See Everything phenomenon goes wide, and Netflix expands its TIFF audience award-winner La Bola Negra .

Sony Pictures Classics opens the Turturro-starring Pickpocket by Noah Segan in limited release on six screens in New York (AMC Lincoln Square, Angelika Film Center, Bam Rose) and Los Angeles (AMC Burbank, AMC Grove, Laemmle Royal). He plays Harry Lehman, an aging pickpocket who plies his trade with ever-diminishing returns in a drastically changed New York.

Related Stories

Deadline’s Reviews Of This Week’s Box Office Openers: ‘Clayface’, ‘Wildwood’ & More

‘Clayface’ Takes Shape As No. 1 With $23M-$25M; ‘You Can See Everything’s Wild Ride Continues With $19M – Box Office Update

Turturro took the Zurich Film Festival’s Golden Eye Award for his performance in the film — Segan’s directorial debut. Steve Buscemi as Harry’s regular fence; Tatiana Maslany as his estranged daughter; and Will Price as the arrogant, heat-packing scion of a Manhattan crime family also star. A favorite out of Sundance where it premiered, the film is Rotten Tomatoes Certified Fresh at 97% . See Deadline’s review , which calls it mesmerizing.

Watch on Deadline

Mubi is out with Paweł Pawlikowski’s Fatherland , also limited, at four theaters in New York (Film Forum, Film at Lincoln Center) and Los Angeles (AMC Burbank, Laemmle Royal). World premiered at Cannes to critical acclaim and the Best Director award for Pawlikowski. At 91% Certified Fresh on Rotten Tomatoes, see Deadline review .

In the summer of 1949, at the height of the Cold War, Nobel Prize-winning writer Thomas Mann (Zischler) and his daughter Erika (Hüller) embark on a challenging and emotional road trip across a Germany in ruins, from U.S.-dominated Frankfurt to Soviet-controlled Weimar. Mann, who had returned home after 16 years in exile in the U.S., faced not only a divided fatherland but also a deep fracture within his own family. Pawlikowski picks up here where he left off with his award-winning Ida and Cold War , exploring themes of identity, family, love and guilt amid the turmoil and confusion of post-war Europe.

Mubi also debuts Making Marie Antoinette , the late filmmaker Eleanor Coppola’s behind-the-scenes documentation of her daughter Sofia Coppola directing 2006 film Marie Antoinette . Premiered at Telluride, Deadline review here . Opens on 20 screens nationally including NY and L.A.

Moderate/wide

Bleecker Street, in partnership with longtime collaborator LD Entertainment, releases Anton Corbijn thriller A Talent For Murder on 876 screens with Helen Mirren starring as celebrated crime novelist Patricia Highsmith. World premiered at TIFF, see Deadline review. Based on Joanna Murray-Smith’s acclaimed 2014 play Switzerland , the film follows a young literary agent from New York (Alden Ehrenreich), who travels to Switzerland on a mission to convince the famously reclusive Highsmith to write one final installment in her iconic Ripley series. What begins as a seemingly straightforward assignment soon takes an unexpected turn.

Black Bear launches Wicker , the Sundance breakout from Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer, at 1,471 theaters. A lusty comedic fable about sex, marriage and social convention centered around a lonely Fisherwoman (Colman), who commissions a wicker husband from the local Basketmaker (Peter Dinklage). Her unexpected romance with the creation (Alexander Skarsgård) sparks jealousy and threatens the village’s social order. The Tailor’s Wife/bullying local queen bee (Elizabeth Debicki) sets out to sabotage the romance. Rotten Tomatoes Certified Fresh at 92% with critics. Audience score of 93%. Deadline review here .

RELATED: How Olivia Colman Starrer ‘Wicker’ Went From Unpublished Short Story To A Big-Screen Feminist Romantasy

Black Bear’s teaser poster/social campaign highlighted an unconventional leading man-turned- object of desire — aka ”What is MARRIAGE MATERIAL, and why is it a basket?” Off that, self-described “basketheads” spread Wicker fandom across the film’s social channels. It had a stunt screening at Beyond Fest, targeted events with Feeld, Letterboxd and Vanity Fair , and events at the 92nd Street Y and Vidiots culminating in the L.A. premiere at the DGA. Fans have been sharing sightings of six-feet-tall Wicker Husband standees in bookstores and theaters. On October 25, it will play in Dolby Cinema at AMC locations nationwide for a daylong event. Black Bear will host a special one-night Wicker 4DX event October 28.

TIFF-premiering documentary Nuns Vs the Vatican by Lorena Luciano debuts at L.A.’s Laemmle Monica Film Center, with a national rollout to follow. Produced by Filippo Piscopo. Mariska Hargitay, Trish Adlesic, Lauran Bromley, Regina K. Scully and Amanda Stephens are executive producers. In the shadows of the Catholic church, nuns and women have long endured abuse at the hands of priests — insidious and tactful grooming, silenced by confession, and hidden through systemic cover-ups. This investigative documentary uncovers the harrowing details and institutional indifference as nuns start to break decades of silence, exposing a system built to protect power. Self-distributed.

article_text:
O novo “X-Men” tem estreia prevista para 5 de maio de 2028.

Em painel agitado durante a D23, a Marvel confirmou o elenco de “ X-Men “, um de seus lançamentos mais aguardados. Adam Driver será o vilão Senhor Sinistro, Christopher Abbott será Charles Xavier/Professor X, Maya Boyd será Ororo Munroe/Tempestade, Inde Navarrette será a Anna Marie/Vampira, Kit Connor será Scott Summers/Ciclope, Samara Weaving será Emma Frost, e Sadie Sink retoma o papel de Jean Grey após “Homem-Aranha: Um Novo Dia”.

O chefão da Marvel nos cinemas, Kevin Feige, ainda confirmou que há mais notícias sobre o elenco de “X-Men” a caminho. A mais óbvia seja talvez a ausência de Erik Lensherr/Magneto, um dos protagonistas da série e principal vilão. Especulava-se que Adam Driver pudesse assumir o papel, algo com que o próprio ator, agora confirmado como Nathaniel Milbury/Senhor Sinistro, brincou em mensagem de vídeo durante o painel:

“Quando Kevin me pediu para aparecer em ‘X-Men’, achei que ele quisesse dizer no set de filmagem. Então, em vez de estar na Califórnia, estou aqui no Pinewood [Studios], neste estúdio de gravação muito solitário. Kevin e eu conversamos durante anos sobre a possibilidade de eu entrar para o Universo Cinematográfico da Marvel. E acho que finalmente encontramos o filme perfeito no momento perfeito. Por isso, estou muito empolgado para interpretar o Mag… Não. Melhor ainda. Nathaniel Milbury. Então, estarei bem aqui, esperando todo mundo chegar.”

O universo “X-Men” é uma das propriedades intelectuais mais populares e lucrativas da Marvel em diversas mídias, incluindo quadrinhos e televisão, mas apenas agora se junta à franquia nos cinemas após a aquisição da 20th Century Fox pela Disney em 2017. Nas mãos da Fox, “X-Men” rendeu sete filmes e uma franquia derivada centrada em Wolverine, com mais três filmes.

No MCU, a primeira aparição de um X-Men se deu em “Doutor Estranho no Multiverso da Loucura”, com Patrick Stewart retomando o papel de Charles Xavier que interpretara nos filmes da Fox. Sadie Sink recentemente interpretou Jean Grey em “Homem-Aranha: Um Novo Dia” e, em “Vingadores: Doutor Destino”, o universo dos X-Men da Fox será enfim concluído com as participações de Stewart novamente, Ian McKellen como Magneto, James Marsden como Ciclope, Rebecca Romijn como Mística e Alan Cumming como Noturno.

Jake Schreier assume a direção do novo “X-Men” após o sucesso de “Thunderbolts*”. O roteiro fica a cargo de Lee Sung Jin, que já trabalhou com Schreier na série “Beef”, e de Joanna Calo.

O novo “X-Men” tem estreia prevista para 5 de maio de 2028.

title_original: Sable Elyse Smith Says Research Isn’t Separate From the Art—It Is the Art
editorial_title_zh: 赛布尔·伊莱斯·史密斯谈研究不独立于艺术——研究本身即是艺术
editorial_excerpt_zh: 在与FLAG艺术基金会“发条”展览相关的一场对话中，史密斯解释了为什么选择材料与创作行为永远密不可分。

"元素的挑选涉及大量的研究。但对我而言，这种研究就是艺术实践。研究是一种持续的专注。我的材料/元素档案馆在不断增长。材料或对象在某种程度上几乎是自给自足的。一个对象可能既是材料又是概念。它所来源的语境可能是主题。当我发现某样东西时，我几乎会为其整个存在建立索引，以向它学习。去了解什么是可能的。它是如何流通的，等等。除了首先询问这里已经存在什么、人们对它通常有什么理解之外，我对待任何事物都没有单一的方法。语言是如何改变它的，然后是一个手势，以此类推。", The material or the object is almost self-contained in a way. An object may be both the material and the concept. The context it comes from might be the subject. When I find something, I almost index the entirety of its existence to learn from it. To learn what is possible. How it circulates, etc. There isn’t just one way I approach anything besides first asking what’s already there, what’s commonly understood about it. Encounters are the catalyst through which we learn, shift, become, recalibrate, create, etc.… and my most profound encounters have been through other’s creative acts (and I don’t just mean the things we call “art” with a capital “A” and have organized an economy around). I mean the most expansive definition of creation or making, willing something into being. So maybe I’m a part of that larger collective impulse. And possibly someone’s encounter with something that I have placed in the world (all my acts of creation, not just what’s in the gallery) in relation to all the other things they have encountered or witnessed will resonate in some sense."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/installation-view-sable-elyse-smith-clockwork-2026-flag-art-foundation-3-768x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Installation view of “Sable Elyse Smith: Clockwork” (2026). article_text:
Sable Elyse Smith has spent the better part of her career investigating the underpinning architecture of power—the furniture, footage, and language through which institutions discipline, surveil, and categorize. On view through February 13, 2027, at the FLAG Art Foundation in New York, “ Clockwork ” builds on the themes of Smith’s earlier show of the same title that was on view at the Contemporary Austin , but through a decidedly new lens.

Curated by FLAG Art Foundation director Jonathan Rider and deputy director Caroline Cassidy , the show marks Smith’s receipt of the 2026 Suzanne Deal Booth / FLAG Art Foundation Prize .

Across sculpture, video, neon, and photography, Smith repurposes objects like prison waiting-room stools and appropriated police footage, using repetition and layering to strip them of their original context and expose the systems that they were built to serve. And a new video work, skin suit (2026), was made specifically for this new presentation.

Ahead of the opening, Smith spoke about reshaping an existing exhibition for a new city and audience, her research-driven approach to materials, and why she resists defining her role as an artist in any single way. Find the conversation, which has been lightly edited for length and clarity, below.

Sable Elyse Smith. Photo: Tommy Kha.

“Clockwork” originated at the Contemporary Austin, and has been reframed by expanding its more cinematic elements. What has that shift in scale allowed you to express that perhaps the earlier presentation could not?

The shift is scale shifts focus. The intimacy of the rooms at FLAG forces you to see differently. And here at FLAG we focused on a sparse hang, again giving full attention to individual moments. Austin had a density which was important to that version of the show, but even still sometimes giving the viewer too many options, a kind of overdrive of frenetic energy, can fracture focus and attention. In that sense, a different narrative thread is able to surface.

Installation view of “Sable Elyse Smith: Clockwork” (2026). Photo: Steven Probert Studio. Courtesy of FLAG Art Foundation.

How did you approach reworking a show that already existed, rather than starting from a blank slate? Did the differences in the cities and their audiences influence any of your choices?

The different cities definitely influenced my choices. That was an easy filter through which to edit down the checklist. I hadn’t previously had a solo show in Austin before, so introducing that audience more to my overall practice was important. New York is familiar with a lot of aspects of my practice, so that made space for many things to be left out. This exhibition could hold gaps and ellipses. Context exists here. I also wanted this show to have breath in-between gestures, space for recognition and then the next work, or the next gesture or room destabilizes that recognition. There is a montage happening in the videos, and I wanted that to be extended to the space as well.

Installation view of “Sable Elyse Smith: Clockwork” (2026). Photo: Steven Probert Studio. Courtesy of FLAG Art Foundation.

Several of the works on view use repetition, doubling, and layering as strategies for obscuring an object’s original meaning. What types of research or processes go into choosing a specific material or object to work with? What informs the ways you materially incorporate them into a work?

Lots of research goes into the selection of elements. But that research is the practice of art for me. The research is an ongoing preoccupation. My archive of material/elements is constantly growing. The material or the object is almost self-contained in a way. An object may be both the material and the concept. The context it comes from might be the subject. When I find something, I almost index the entirety of its existence to learn from it. To learn what is possible. How it circulates, etc. There isn’t just one way I approach anything besides first asking what’s already there, what’s commonly understood about it. How does language shift it, then a gesture, and so on and so forth.

Video still from Sable Elyse Smith, skin suit (2026). Courtesy of FLAG Art Foundation.

skin suit (2026) was made specifically for this prize and exhibition. Did the context (a stage-set environment at FLAG) influence how you created it?

The exhibition venues did not influence the making of the work. The work influenced what was possible in space, and an opportunity to expand the world in which video making is birthed. Image, circulation, context, text, space, and resonance. I think it allows for some seepage.

Alex Klein, the head curator and director of curatorial affairs at the Contemporary Austin, described your work as revealing that “the mechanisms of social control we often take for granted are in fact by design.” Do you see your role as an artist primarily as one of exposure, or do you see the work as doing something beyond that?

I have not defined what my role as an artist is to a subtitle or subheading. I’m a person who tries to pay attention in the world, and I process that through these creative impulses. That’s important to me, and there seems to be a collective drive to do so. Encounters are the catalyst through which we learn, shift, become, recalibrate, create, etc.… and my most profound encounters have been through other’s creative acts (and I don’t just mean the things we call “art” with a capital “A” and have organized an economy around). I mean the most expansive definition of creation or making, willing something into being. So maybe I’m a part of that larger collective impulse. And possibly someone’s encounter with something that I have placed in the world (all my acts of creation, not just what’s in the gallery) in relation to all the other things they have encountered or witnessed will resonate in some sense.

Installation view of “Sable Elyse Smith: Clockwork” (2026). Photo: Steven Probert Studio. Courtesy of FLAG Art Foundation.

Taking into consideration the full arc of “Clockwork”—sculpture, video, neon, photography—what do you hope visitors take away from the show on the whole versus any singular piece?

I don’t know; maybe an understanding of my relationship to language and writing. These are all proxies in a way.

“ Sable Elyse Smith: Clockwork ” is on view at the FLAG Art Foundation, New York, through February 13, 2027.

コミュニティ論

映画館を探す

予告編を見る

U-NEXTで 関連作品を見る PR

解説・あらすじ

映画監督・映像ディレクター・プロデューサー・作家・ミュージシャン・デザイナーなど多彩なメンバーが在籍するクリエイターユニット「P-kraft」が制作したオムニバス映画。P-kraftに所属する作家・関口純の書き下ろし短編3本を原作に、さまざまなコミュニティが小さな嘘や見栄によって思いがけない方向へと展開していく様子を、3人の監督がそれぞれ異なるアプローチで描き出す。 社会学のフィールドワークで平凡な田舎町に移住した真面目すぎる大学院生と、彼をからかおうと悪ふざけをヒートアップさせていく町民たちを描く「社会学者の調査」、好意を寄せる同僚が映画好きだと知った無趣味な会社員が、無名の映画監督の上映会で映画通のフリをしたことから思わぬ困難に陥っていく「消えた日曜日」、思い入れのある市立図書館の閉鎖を告げられた市役所職員が、図書館を救うためにでっちあげた流行語で想定外の大ブームを巻き起こしてしまう「神様は、どこ？」の3作品で構成。 監督を担うのは、P-kraft代表を務める映像ディレクターの板部文、映画美術デザイナーの安藤秀敏、映像学校講師も務める映画監督の笹木惠水。

2026年製作／126分／日本 配給：P-kraft 劇場公開日：2026年11月6日

article_text:
The Latino Film Institute has unveiled its seventh annual cohort of directors for the LFI Inclusion Fellowship supported by Netflix.

Ten emerging filmmakers join the program to produce live-action narrative short films through $50,000 production grants, mentorship and industry engagement opportunities. Fellows participate in a studio-style environment and will screen their completed films at the Los Angeles Latino International Film Festival.

Related Stories

Music Industry Moves: My Chemical Romance Signs With Warner Chappell

Agencies and Producers Back U.S. Tax Incentive as 'First Step' Toward Hollywood Recovery

“Netflix’s continued commitment to the LFI Inclusion Fellowship makes a real difference for filmmakers with bold, original stories to tell,” said Diana Cadavid, director of industry programs at the Latino Film Institute. “This year’s cohort spans horror, coming-of-age, comedy, romance, sci-fi and drama and every project stands out for its visual ambition and conceptual strength. Through mentorship, resources and direct industry access, we’re supporting the selected filmmakers to bring their visions to the screen and opening doors for the advancement of their careers.”

The fellows will also participate in LALIFF Connect: Market & Creative Forum, the festival’s professional development and networking section. There, the cohort will be able to network with industry professionals in production, distribution, acquisitions and representation.

The 2027 LFI cohort is: Adalberto Angulo — “Saboteur” Alexander Ibarra — “Mariposa Muere” Berman Fenelus — “The Last Hive” Camila de Ilhéus — “d’Aparecida” Crystal Ferreiro — “PUMPED!” Jasmin Prophete — “Zonbi” Kevin Rios — “Hurricane Mima” María Sofía Hernández — “El Turno (Carpool)” Mariales Diaz — “Tío dice que te suelte en banda (Don’t Hold Me Close)” Miguel Ortiz — “Brother Bushi”

Since forming, the fellowship has launched 55 alumni in producing films that have premiered at major festivals and secured distribution.
